summary:
AURA AstroVitals is an offline-first health-monitoring prototype for astronauts, built by Team Interstellar Overdrive for the challenge “Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions.”
On long missions, such as a trip to Mars, messages to Earth can take up to about 44 minutes for a round trip and can be blocked for weeks. A crew cannot always wait for help from the ground, so AURA helps astronauts understand their own health on board.
AURA brings together body signals, daily check-ins, and cabin conditions such as CO₂, temperature and noise. It compares each astronaut with their own normal, not with Earth averages. Its main safety rule is: “The models advise. The rules decide.” Only clear, readable rules reviewed by medical staff can raise an official alert. Small AI models run quietly in the background and can only post labelled advisory notices, such as a slow drift in heart rate and sleep, or a short trend forecast with its uncertainty.
Future crews will be far from Earth, and a tool that works without a connection and keeps rules in charge of alerts can help them notice problems early.
details:
What it does
AURA AstroVitals is a health-monitoring prototype for astronauts on long missions, when help from Earth is delayed or cut off. It gathers body signals (heart rate, heart-rate variability, sleep, activity, skin temperature), a short daily check-in (mood, fatigue, pain, hydration, symptoms) and cabin readings (CO₂, temperature, humidity, noise, light, radiation level). It shows each astronaut’s status, any alerts or notices, and the reason behind them, all on local equipment without needing the cloud.
How it works
Every reading is checked first. A missing, frozen or impossible value gives a “sensor problem” message, not a false health alert.
Each astronaut is compared with their own recent normal, not with Earth averages, because spaceflight changes the body.
Rules lane: clear, readable rules, written and reviewed by medical teammates, can raise official alerts. Each alert shows which rule fired and a suggested checklist.
Advisory lane: four small machine-learning models run quietly on the local computer. One looks for unusual combined changes in the body, one for unusual cabin conditions, one gives a low/moderate/elevated risk band for heart and fitness decline, and one forecasts resting heart rate, heart-rate variability and sleep for the next 7–14 days with an uncertainty band. They can only post labelled advisory notices (“not a diagnosis”, no alarm sound), and only after a pattern persists across several checks.
If a model fails, only that model is switched off and the rules keep running.
The guiding principle is: “The models advise. The rules decide.”
Benefits and intended impact
Crews get a clear picture of their own health when Earth is far away.
People stay in control: the AI never raises official alerts, and every alert has a readable reason.
Fewer false alarms, because each person is compared with their own normal and bad sensors are flagged.
We hope AURA shows a safe, explainable design pattern that medical and engineering experts can review, test and improve. It is a prototype and a starting point, not a finished medical system.
What makes it creative
Splitting decisions into a rules lane and an advisory AI lane, with a firm limit on what the AI may do.
Designing for real space limits: no cloud, small models on local equipment, and queued messages for Earth.
Training and testing the AI on a simulator of virtual astronauts with known ground truth, so we can measure whether the models catch problems we injected. We label this clearly as simulated.
Honest labelling in the interface: advisory notices, official alerts, bad-sensor messages and “model unavailable” each look different.
Factors the team considered
Communication delay and blackouts (up to about 44 minutes round trip, and weeks without contact).
Limited power, memory and computing on board.
Safety: AI must not diagnose or trigger alarms alone.
Evidence: we based our choices on NASA reports and published studies, and we state what is not proven.
Privacy and consent for sensitive mood and behavioural data.
Sensor quality, because a bad reading should not look like a health problem.
Tools used
[Website languages and frameworks] · [Python libraries for the simulator and models; model types such as Isolation Forest or One-Class SVM, and LSTM/GRU or a trend baseline] · [Hosting, repository] · [Hardware, or “runs in a standard web browser”] · SI tools are listed in the AI/SI section.
Working features, limits and future plans
Working now: [list exactly what judges can open and use] and the simulator with four AI models trained and tested on it.
Limits: The AI was trained and tested only on simulated astronauts, so results show behaviour on simulated scenarios only. AURA is not a medical device, is not clinically validated and does not diagnose. Rule thresholds are starting examples that need review by medical experts. Sensor data are simulated, and real hardware is not connected.

Future plans (not built): context detection, signal-quality and sensor cross-checks, circadian monitoring, offline voice check-in, camera-assisted exercise and fatigue checks, a shared-cause crew check, and a radiation event screen.
